      On June 10, 2025, McKenzie Electric Cooperative, Inc. filed a complaint

against Basin Electric Power Cooperative in Docket No. EL25-92-000

(“Complaint”). Ex. A, at 1. On June 30, 2025, Tri-State timely intervened and filed

comments in the Complaint proceeding. See id. at 8.

      On May 21, 2026, the Commission issued the Initial Order denying the

Complaint. Ex. A. On June 22, 2026, Tri-State timely sought rehearing of the Initial

Order. See Ex. B. On July 23, 2026, the Commission issued the Rehearing Denial

Order, which does not address the substance of Petitioner’s rehearing request but

deemed the request denied pursuant to 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a) and this Court’s decision

in Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC, 964 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2020) (en banc). Ex.

B.

      Petitioner now seeks review of the Initial Order and the Rehearing Denial

Order before this Court. Because Petitioner’s June 22, 2026 request for rehearing is

deemed to have been denied on July 23, 2026, this petition for review is timely.

Venue is proper under 16 U.S.C. § 825l(b). Copies of the challenged orders are

attached as Exhibits A and B.

      Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court hold unlawful, vacate, enjoin,

and set aside the Commission’s orders and grand such further relief as may be

appropriate.

                               ORDER DENYING COMPLAINT

                                   (Issued May 21, 2026)

       On June 10, 2025, as supplemented on July 2, 2025, 1 McKenzie Electric
Cooperative, Inc. (McKenzie) filed a complaint under sections 306 and 309 2 of the
Federal Power Act (FPA) and Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and
Procedure, 3 against Basin Electric Power Cooperative (Basin) alleging that Basin has
engaged in a nominal and “sham transaction” with the Rural Utilities Service (RUS)
(RUS Transaction) by taking on a $928,000 loan (RUS Loan) allegedly for the purpose
of evading the jurisdiction of the Commission in violation of the FPA (Complaint).
McKenzie requests that the Commission find that the RUS Transaction is void or
ineffective for jurisdictional purposes, is inconsistent with section 204 4 of the FPA, and
requests that the Commission confirm its regulatory authority over Basin and the affected
assets or services. 5 As discussed below, we deny the Complaint.

I.     Background

       A.        McKenzie

       McKenzie states that it is a member-owned rural electric cooperative that serves
residential, commercial, and industrial member-owners in North Dakota and Montana. It
further explains that it is a Class C member of Basin and purchases the entirety of its
power requirements via Upper Missouri G. & T. Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Upper
Missouri), which is a Class A member of Basin. McKenzie also states that it is the
largest by load of the 11 member-owners of Upper Missouri. Additionally, McKenzie
explains that all-requirements documents establishing this Basin-Upper Missouri-
McKenzie power purchasing relationship expire in 2075, and that the primary component
of McKenzie’s costs for electric service is Basin’s Rate Schedule A for all-requirements
service. McKenzie explains that the Rate Schedule A rates are passed through to
McKenzie in Upper Missouri’s rates and that McKenzie allocates the costs to its own
member-owners through retail rates. 6

       B.        Basin

        McKenzie states that Basin is a not-for-profit, consumer-owned rural electric
generation and transmission (G&T) cooperative in North Dakota and was founded by
member-owned cooperatives in North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Montana, and
Iowa. It states that Basin’s purpose is to provide the additional electric power and energy
needed by those cooperatives and their members, over and above their historic power
allocations from the Western Area Power Administration. McKenzie further states that
Basin operates approximately 5,200 megawatts of electric generating capacity and has
approximately 8,100 megawatts of capacity in its generation portfolio. Additionally,
McKenzie states that Basin provides supplemental wholesale power to 140 rural electric
member systems in Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North
Dakota, South Dakota, and Wyoming. McKenzie asserts that because Basin controls
virtually all of the power generation available to approximately three million member-
consumers across nine states, its transmission and electric energy sales are “materially
equivalent to some of the largest public utilities in the nation.” 7

      McKenzie states that in June 2024, a presiding Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) at
the Commission issued an initial decision that determined that the rates Basin charged its
members for wholesale energy throughout the 2020 and 2021 rate years were unjust,
unreasonable, and unlawful because, in part, Basin’s rates included amounts used to
recover the significant losses incurred by its nonutility subsidiary, Dakota Gasification

      C.         Basin’s Jurisdictional Status, Prior RUS Debt and RUS Loan

       Until November 2019, Basin was exempt from the Commission’s jurisdiction
under section 201(f) of the FPA 10 because it either held RUS debt or was wholly owned
by entities that were themselves exempt from the Commission’s jurisdiction under
section 201(f) of the FPA. Section 201(f) of the FPA provides an exemption from
Commission jurisdiction for cooperatives that obtain RUS financing. It provides:

                 No provision in this subchapter shall apply to, or be deemed
                 to include, the United States, a State or any political
                 subdivision of a State, an electric cooperative that receives
                 financing under the Rural Electrification Act of 1936 (7
                 U.S.C. 901 et seq.) or that sells less than 4,000,000 megawatt
                 hours of electricity per year, or any agency, authority, or
                 instrumentality of any one or more of the foregoing . . . unless
                 such provision makes specific reference thereto. 11

Thus, Basin was not a “public utility” as defined in section 201(e) of the FPA and was
exempt from Commission regulation by virtue of section 201(f). 12

       In early 2015, Basin refinanced $1.2 billion in previously borrowed RUS debt with
private lenders. In November 2019, Basin did not otherwise qualify for the exemption
under section 201(f) because one or more of its Class A members ceased to qualify for
the section 201(f) exemption. 13 On January 16, 2025, the RUS approved Basin’s

       D.       Section 204 Authorization

II.    Complaint

       McKenzie alleges that Basin is attempting to evade the Commission’s jurisdiction
through the RUS Transaction. 20 McKenzie argues that the Commission’s role under
section 204 is not merely ministerial and that the courts have consistently granted
agencies discretion in interpreting broad statutory language, such as the phrase
“compatible with the public interest” in section 204. 21 It contends that section 204
must be read in harmony with the provisions in sections 205 and 206 that grant the
Commission comprehensive authority to ensure just and reasonable rates and to remedy
unjust practices. Specifically, McKenzie maintains that section 204 should be read to
protect the Commission’s jurisdiction from public utilities’ efforts to forum shop and
avoid public scrutiny, especially where, as here, such scrutiny has already revealed
unlawful rates. McKenzie asserts that judicial interpretations of section 204 have
confirmed the Commission’s responsibilities to consider a wide range of factors,
including financial integrity and anticompetitive effects when authorizing liabilities to be
incurred by a utility. 22

V.    Substantive Matters

       As discussed below, we deny the Complaint. In this proceeding, McKenzie and

authorize an issuance of securities or assumption of liability only if it finds that such
issue or assumption is for a lawful object, within the corporate purposes of the applicant
and compatible with the public interest, and is reasonably necessary or appropriate for
such purposes. 131
